consensus_summary: Iron primarily symbolizes strength, hardness, and unyielding/crushing power (especially of kingdoms, rule, or judgment, via the rod of iron and Daniel’s fourth kingdom), with common secondary senses of oppression/bondage (iron yoke or furnace) and minority senses of stubbornness or mutual sharpening.
book_summary: Iron is identified as the fourth kingdom—Rome—the empire that breaks in pieces all before it and that held the world when Christ came, following the outright naming of Medo-Persia and Greece.
consensus_core_identification: strength/hardness/unyielding power (of rule or kingdoms), with Daniel’s iron fourth kingdom as a key application
boundary_disagreement: Book elevates and restricts the term to the single historical identification of Daniel’s fourth kingdom as Rome, excluding the broader consensus applications (messianic rod of iron, iron furnace/yoke as affliction, hardness of heart, iron-sharpens-iron, etc.).
material_contradiction: None; the book’s identification is already present as a common consensus application of the Daniel imagery and does not deny iron’s association with strength.
rationale: Consensus cores on the general quality of unyielding strength, treating the fourth kingdom as one prominent (often common) example or alternative rather than the exclusive sense. The book preserves that Danielic referent but narrows its extension and precision to Rome alone as the meaning of iron, producing boundary disagreement without replacing the central category or introducing contradiction or novelty.
strongest_objection: Consensus regards the fourth-kingdom sense as one contextual application among several, not the sole or primary meaning of the multivalent image ‘iron’.
